blocks.text: PCA, principal component analysis, takes a dataset with many columns and finds a much smaller number of new directions that still capture almost everything interesting about it. This lesson pulls together nearly every idea from this module, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, orthogonality, projection, and SVD, into the single most widely used dimensionality reduction technique in applied machine learning.

blocks.alt: The PCA pipeline, step by step
blocks.caption: Each stage of PCA reuses a concept already covered earlier in this module

blocks.text: 1. What PCA Is Trying to Do

Real datasets often have columns that overlap heavily in the information they carry, height in centimeters and height in inches, or several correlated financial indicators. PCA searches for a small number of new, artificial directions, called principal components, that between them capture as much of the original spread, or variance, in the data as possible.

blocks.alt: A scatter of points and its dominant direction
blocks.caption: The blue line is the direction along which the points spread out the most

blocks.text: Once that dominant direction is found, describing each point by how far along it sits, rather than by its original two or more coordinates, can capture most of the useful structure using far fewer numbers.

PCA never invents new information, it only reorganizes existing information into a more efficient set of directions, choosing to keep the ones that capture the most spread and setting aside the ones that add little beyond what is already known.
2. Step 1: Center the Data

Before anything else, PCA subtracts the average value of each column from every entry in that column, so the dataset is recentered around the origin. This step matters because the covariance calculation in step 2 only measures spread relative to the mean, not relative to zero.

code.content:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[2, 8], [4, 10], [6, 12], [8, 14]])
X_centered = X - X.mean(axis=0)
print(X_centered)   # each column now has mean 0

blocks.text: 3. Step 2: The Covariance Matrix

The covariance matrix summarizes how every pair of columns varies together, and is always symmetric, guaranteeing, by the eigenvalues and orthogonality lessons, real eigenvalues and mutually perpendicular eigenvectors.

code.content:
cov = np.cov(X_centered.T)
print(cov)   # a symmetric matrix, one row and column per original feature

blocks.text: A large off diagonal value in this matrix signals two columns rise and fall together strongly, exactly the kind of redundancy PCA is designed to consolidate into fewer, cleaner directions.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A covariance value close to 0 between two columns means they vary largely independently of one another, while a large positive covariance means they tend to rise and fall together, both signals PCA uses when deciding how to combine columns into new, decorrelated directions.

blocks.text: 4. Step 3: Eigenvectors as New Axes

The eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, covered in the eigenvectors lesson, become the new candidate axes for describing the data, called principal components. Because the covariance matrix is symmetric, these eigenvectors are automatically orthogonal to one another, exactly as guaranteed by the orthogonality lesson.

code.content:
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eig(cov)
print(eigenvectors.T.dot(eigenvectors))   # close to the identity, confirming orthogonality

blocks.text: It is worth pausing on how directly this reuses the eigenvectors lesson: nothing new is being introduced here mathematically, PCA is simply eigen decomposition applied specifically to a covariance matrix, with a specific interpretation, variance direction, attached to the result.
5. Step 4: Eigenvalues Rank the Axes by Variance

Each eigenvalue tells you how much variance, how much spread in the original data, lies along its matching eigenvector. Sorting eigenvalues from largest to smallest, exactly as the eigenvalues lesson demonstrated, ranks the new axes from most informative to least.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Component","Eigenvalue","Share of total variance"],"rows":[["first principal component","9.2","about 92 percent"],["second principal component","0.8","about 8 percent"]]}

blocks.text: This ranking is the single most important output PCA produces, it tells you exactly how many of the new axes are worth keeping before meaningfully losing information.
6. Projecting Data onto Principal Components
Once the top principal components are chosen, every data point gets projected onto them, using the exact projection formula from the projection lesson, to produce its new, reduced set of coordinates.

code.content:
top_k = eigenvectors[:, np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1][:1]]   # keep only the top 1 eigenvector
reduced = X_centered.dot(top_k)
print(reduced.shape)   # (4, 1), 2 original columns compressed down to 1

blocks.text: Because the principal components are orthogonal, this projection can be done one component at a time using a plain dot product, with no need for the fuller subspace projection matrix machinery covered in the projection lesson.
6.1 What the Reduced Coordinates Mean

Each reduced coordinate is simply how far along that principal component direction the point sits, exactly the scalar projection idea from the projection lesson, now applied using the covariance eigenvectors as the target directions instead of an arbitrary vector.
7. Choosing How Many Components to Keep

The explained variance ratio from section 5 directly guides how many components to keep, following the same explained variance logic the SVD lesson introduced for choosing a truncation rank k. A common rule of thumb is to keep enough components to explain at least 90 or 95 percent of the total variance.

code.content:
total_variance = np.sum(eigenvalues)
explained_ratio = np.sort(eigenvalues)[::-1] / total_variance
cumulative = np.cumsum(explained_ratio)
k = np.searchsorted(cumulative, 0.95) + 1

blocks.text: Plotting the individual and cumulative explained variance ratio against the number of components, sometimes called a scree plot, is a common visual habit for spotting the point where additional components stop adding meaningful new information.
8. PCA in Practice with a Library

In real projects, PCA is rarely hand rolled the way sections 2 through 6 walked through, a well tested library implementation is used instead, but every step it performs internally is exactly what was just covered.

code.content:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
model = PCA(n_components=1)
reduced = model.fit_transform(X)
print(model.explained_variance_ratio_)   # matches the ranking from section 5

blocks.text: 9. PCA via SVD

The SVD lesson mentioned that PCA is usually computed via SVD directly on the centered data matrix, rather than by explicitly building a covariance matrix first, for better numerical stability. The singular values from that SVD are directly proportional to the standard deviations along each principal component.

code.content:
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X_centered, full_matrices=False)
principal_components = Vt   # same directions eigen decomposition of the covariance matrix would find
reduced_via_svd = U * S    # equivalent reduced coordinates

blocks.text: This is why most production PCA implementations, including the one used in section 8, default to an SVD based computation under the hood rather than the eigen decomposition path walked through step by step earlier in this lesson.

Both routes, eigen decomposition of the covariance matrix or direct SVD of the centered data, produce the same principal directions in theory, the SVD route is simply preferred in practice for the numerical stability reasons already covered in the SVD lesson.
10. Reconstructing Data from PCA

Multiplying the reduced coordinates back by the kept principal components, then adding the original mean back, approximately reconstructs the original data, with an error that grows the fewer components were kept, matching the low rank approximation tradeoff from the SVD lesson.

code.content:
reconstructed = reduced.dot(top_k.T) + X.mean(axis=0)
print(np.linalg.norm(X - reconstructed))   # how much information the 1-component reduction lost

blocks.text: Comparing the reconstruction error across different values of k is a practical way to decide, empirically, how aggressive a reduction a specific dataset can tolerate before the loss becomes noticeable for whatever task the reduced data will be used for.
11. PCA in AI Practice

items: Visualizing high dimensional embeddings by reducing them to 2 or 3 principal components, a common first step when trying to inspect what a model has learned.
Speeding up downstream model training by feeding in a smaller number of principal components instead of hundreds of raw, correlated features.
Denoising sensor or signal data, where the low variance components frequently correspond to noise rather than genuine signal, and can be safely dropped.
Preprocessing image data before feeding it into classical machine learning models that do not natively handle very high dimensional raw pixel inputs well.

blocks.text: These use cases share a common thread: whenever a downstream step struggles with too many correlated or noisy dimensions, PCA offers a principled way to shrink that dimensionality first, without hand picking which original features to drop.
12. What PCA Does Not Do

PCA only rotates and reduces the existing feature space, it does not select a subset of the original, human interpretable features, the new axes are combinations of all of them, which can make the reduced components harder to explain directly. PCA also assumes the interesting structure in the data is linear, and it is sensitive to the scale of each feature, since a feature measured in the thousands will dominate the variance calculation over one measured in single digits unless features are standardized first.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A dataset with income in dollars and age in years, left unstandardized, will have PCA dominated almost entirely by income simply because its raw numeric values are so much larger, not because income is actually more informative. Standardizing both columns to comparable scales before running PCA avoids this distortion.

blocks.text: 13. Standardizing Before the Covariance Step

The scale sensitivity flagged in section 12 has a standard fix: subtract each column mean, as in section 2, then additionally divide each column by its own standard deviation, so every feature contributes on a comparable scale before the covariance matrix is built.

code.content:
X_standardized = (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0)
model = PCA(n_components=2)
reduced = model.fit_transform(X_standardized)

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Standardizing income measured in the thousands and age measured in single digits brings both onto the same footing, roughly mean 0 and standard deviation 1, so PCA can weigh their actual correlational structure rather than being dominated by whichever column happened to have larger raw numbers.

blocks.text: 14. A Worked Example
Reduce a small 4 point, 2 feature dataset down to 1 principal component and check how much variance is retained.

code.content:
X = np.array([[2, 8], [4, 10], [6, 12], [8, 14]])   # perfectly correlated columns
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
model = PCA(n_components=1)
reduced = model.fit_transform(X)
print(model.explained_variance_ratio_)   # [1.], 100 percent, since the 2 columns carry identical information

blocks.text: This dataset was constructed so the second column is always exactly 3 plus twice the first, a perfectly redundant relationship, which is why a single principal component captures all of the variance without any loss at all.

A real dataset almost never reaches exactly 100 percent explained variance with fewer components than it started with, this example was deliberately constructed with perfect redundancy to make the underlying mechanism as visible as possible.
15. Common Mistakes

items: Skipping standardization on features with very different scales, letting a single large-magnitude column dominate every principal component regardless of its actual importance.
Forgetting to center the data first, which the covariance calculation in section 3 depends on to measure spread correctly.
Treating principal components as directly interpretable original features, they are combinations of all the original columns, not a subset of them.
Keeping too few components purely to hit a round number of dimensions, rather than checking the explained variance from section 7 to see how much information that choice actually discards.

blocks.text: Another trap worth naming directly: assuming PCA improves every downstream model automatically, for some tasks, especially ones where the discarded low variance directions actually carried the signal that mattered, PCA can quietly hurt performance rather than help it.
16. Practice: Run PCA and Check Variance
Take a small dataset with 3 features where one feature is simply the sum of the other two, run PCA keeping 2 components, and confirm the explained variance ratio shows the redundancy clearly.

code.content:
X = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 5], [3, 1, 4], [4, 4, 8]])
model = PCA(n_components=2)
reduced = model.fit_transform(X)
print(model.explained_variance_ratio_)   # 2 components should already explain close to 100 percent

items: Confirming the explained variance is near 100 percent with only 2 of the 3 original columns reproduces, in a concrete case, exactly the redundancy detection idea introduced back in the rank of matrix lesson.

blocks.text: Try the same exercise again after standardizing the 3 columns first, using the technique from section 12.5, and compare whether the explained variance ratio changes noticeably from the unstandardized version.
Key Takeaway

Standardizing before PCA, from section 12.5, is a step worth applying by default whenever the original features are not already on comparable scales, skipping it silently biases the result toward whichever columns happen to have larger raw magnitudes.

PCA finds new, orthogonal directions, ranked by how much variance they capture, using the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of a dataset covariance matrix, or equivalently the SVD of the centered data itself. Keeping only the top few of those directions compresses a dataset while preserving as much of its useful structure as possible.

This lesson closes out the Linear Algebra module by tying together nearly everything covered so far: eigenvalues and eigenvectors supply the ranked directions, orthogonality guarantees those directions do not overlap, projection extracts the reduced coordinates, and SVD offers the more numerically robust way to compute the whole thing in one step.

Every earlier lesson in this Linear Algebra module was, in some sense, building toward this one: vectors and matrices gave the language, dot products and norms gave the tools to measure length and overlap, and eigenvalues, orthogonality, projection, and SVD gave the machinery PCA assembles into a single, practical technique.
